mainEntity.name: Can I continue wearing a cracked denture if it is not causing pain?

acceptedAnswer.text: Even if a cracked denture is not causing immediate pain, it is not advisable to continue wearing it without professional assessment. A crack weakens the structural integrity of the appliance, meaning further breakage is more likely. Cracks also make thorough cleaning difficult, potentially harbouring bacteria or fungi. A dental professional can advise on whether repair or replacement is the most appropriate course of action based on the extent of the damage and the condition of the denture overall.

mainEntity.name: How quickly should I see a dentist if my denture breaks?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is advisable to contact your dental practice as soon as possible after a denture breaks. Many practices can offer advice over the telephone and may be able to arrange an urgent or same-day appointment if you are in pain or unable to wear the appliance. Professional denture repair is usually far more durable than temporary home solutions, and prompt assessment can prevent secondary problems from developing in the soft tissues of the mouth.

mainEntity.name: Is it safe to use denture adhesive with a damaged denture?

acceptedAnswer.text: Denture adhesive may provide very short-term stability improvement, but it is not a safe or appropriate solution for a damaged denture. Adhesive cannot restore the structural integrity of a cracked base or replace a broken clasp. Using adhesive to compensate for a poorly fitting or damaged denture can mask symptoms that may need professional attention and can make it more difficult to assess the underlying issue when you do attend for an appointment.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I leave a poorly fitting denture unaddressed for a long time?

acceptedAnswer.text: Wearing a poorly fitting denture over a prolonged period can contribute to accelerated bone resorption beneath the denture, chronic soft tissue irritation, and changes in the shape of the gum ridges. These changes can make future denture fitting more challenging. In some cases, persistent trauma from an ill-fitting denture can lead to thickened tissue (denture-induced hyperplasia) that may require treatment before a new denture can be fitted successfully. Early assessment helps to avoid these longer-term complications.

mainEntity.name: Can dentures be repaired rather than replaced?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes — a dental technician working with your dentist can repair cracked acrylic bases, replace broken denture teeth, and adjust clasps on partial dentures. However, the suitability of repair depends on the extent of the damage, the age of the appliance, and whether the underlying fit remains acceptable. A denture that has been repaired multiple times may have a weakened structure. Your dental professional can advise on whether repair or replacement represents the better long-term solution for your individual situation.

mainEntity.name: How often should dentures be professionally assessed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental guidance generally suggests that denture wearers attend for a dental review at least once per year, even in the absence of obvious problems. During these reviews, the dentist can assess the condition and fit of the denture, examine the oral soft tissues, and monitor for any changes in the gum ridges or bite. Early identification of fit changes allows for timely adjustment or relining, which can extend the lifespan of the appliance and prevent discomfort from developing.
